title: The Epiphany
hookLine: the magi's gifts: gold for a king, frankincense for God, myrrh for death

cards: In early January, above some front doors in Poland, in Germany, in Catholic neighborhoods of the American Midwest, there are letters and numbers chalked on the frame: the year, split in two, with C, M and B in between and little crosses.
The letters stand for a Latin blessing, Christ bless this house, and for the three names legend gave the wise men, Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar. The chalk goes up on today's feast.
And much of the popular picture of those men isn't in the Bible.

teach.b: Matthew calls them magoi, magi, a word Greek writers used for Persian priests and star-watchers. He never says there were three, and he never calls them kings.
Later tradition counted three from the three gifts, borrowed crowns from a psalm about kings bringing presents, and gave them names.
What Matthew does say: they came from the east, following a star, asking, where is he that is born king of the Jews?

They find the child with Mary his mother, they fall down and adore him, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "they offered him gifts; gold, frankincense, and myrrh." Early Christian writers read the gifts as a little creed.
Gold, for a king. Frankincense, the incense burned in the temple, for God. Myrrh, a resin used to anoint the dead, for a man who would die.
Myrrh comes back at the end of John's gospel, when Nicodemus brings a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds, to the tomb.
Epiphany comes from the Greek epiphaneia, an appearing or showing: God made visible, and here made visible to outsiders, foreigners not of Israel, who read the sky and came a long way.
In the Latin West the feast centers on the magi; Eastern churches center the same January feast on the baptism in the Jordan.
It's traditionally kept on January 6, the twelfth day after Christmas, though in the United States it moves to the Sunday between January 2 and 8.

how: Catholics keep the Epiphany on January 6 or, in the United States and some other countries, on the Sunday between January 2 and 8; some families have their homes blessed and chalk the doorframe that day.

games.q: you're one of the magi. after a long journey you've found the child with Mary his mother. what do you do first?
o: ask Herod to come and see.
fall down and adore him, then open your treasures.
leave the gifts at the door and go.
games.why: they fall down and adore him, then offer gold, frankincense and myrrh. then they go home another way.

practice: Choose one person outside your usual circle, the person who cleans your office, a neighbor you barely know, a stranger far away, and a small gift for them: a note, a coffee, an hour of help.
The magi came from outside; let your gift go outside too. If you pray, offer it as they did.

wordCard.voice: The Epiphany. From the Greek for a showing: the feast of the magi, when Christ is made known to the nations. Today's word.
